title: ETS2: do we know what we want to measure and achieve?
text:
From 2028 the European Union will put a price on CO₂ emissions from heating buildings and from motor fuels. Allowances in the new emissions trading system, ETS2, will be bought not by households but by fuel suppliers1. The costs will, however, feed through to prices: by our calculation, the average Czech household will pay €218 a year more for energy in 2032 because of ETS2, just under one per cent of its net income2. This year the EU postponed the start of the system by a year3, and Czechia and Italy are now pushing for it to be suspended4.
If ETS2 does go ahead, the state will earn new revenue from selling allowances, which it must spend on climate and social measures5. Before we decide what to do with that money, we should be clear about two things: what we want to achieve, and how we will know that we have achieved it. The answer to the first question lies in the situation Europe is in. For the second, our research helps: the indicators by which success will be judged can assess the same support in very different ways.

title: ETS2: do we know what we want to measure and achieve?
text:
What we want to achieve
Reducing CO₂ emissions is a sensible goal. But Europe pursues it from a weaker starting position than its competitors.
Energy in Europe is expensive, and we import most of it. The 2024 Draghi report on the future of European competitiveness states that EU companies pay two to three times more for electricity than companies in the US, and four to five times more for natural gas. It names Europe’s lack of natural resources as the main cause, but also flaws in the common energy market and high taxes. And it warns that if Europe fails to coordinate its policies, decarbonisation risks running contrary to competitiveness and growth6. In 2024 the EU imported 57% of the energy available to it, and two thirds of these imports were oil and petroleum products7.
Our main competitors do not impose the same costs on themselves. Since January 2026 the United States has not been a party to the Paris Agreement8, and it has declared a “national energy emergency” to expand domestic energy production, including oil and natural gas9. China has an emissions trading system, but for now it does not tell firms how much they may emit in total10.
Regulation comes on top of expensive energy. According to the Draghi report, more than 60% of EU companies see it as an obstacle to investment11. Between 2019 and 2024 the EU passed around 13,000 acts, while around 3,500 laws and 2,000 resolutions were adopted at federal level in the US12. An overall figure for how much regulation adds to the price of European products is missing13. Partial estimates do exist: EU legislation from 2004 to 2014 cost the chemical industry about 2% of its turnover and 12% of its value added, roughly one euro in every eight that the sector itself created14.
Some of the regulation we add ourselves. In October this year the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, proposed a “pact against overregulation”: member states should show which obligations come from EU law and which they have added themselves15. Czechia has improved as far as new laws are concerned: under a 2016 government methodology it transposes directives in their minimal form, and unjustified gold-plating has almost disappeared from new legislation16. It persists, however, in older laws, in MPs’ amendments and in practice17. For example, when a building that was built and last substantially altered before 1947 is sold or let, no energy performance certificate is needed if both parties agree in writing18. According to an analysis by the Association for International Affairs (AMO), however, the media and firms that prepare such assessments often keep quiet about exemptions of this kind19. Exemptions that spare people administrative burden are welcome; people must, however, be made aware of them. According to the Czech Chamber of Commerce, administration costs Czech businesses around CZK 72 billion a year20.
So what do we want to achieve? For the EU and Czechia to depend less on imported fossil fuels, which is the right thing to do regardless of the climate, and for products made in Europe not to be made more expensive by unnecessary rules. ETS2 money can contribute to this, but that depends on where it goes and on how its contribution will be judged.

title: ETS2: do we know what we want to measure and achieve?
section: How we will know it is working
text:
How we will know it is working
The rules for ETS2 money have two parts. Revenue from some of the allowances goes to the EU’s Social Climate Fund, from which Czechia can receive up to CZK 50 billion over 2026 to 203221. The state must add at least a quarter of the costs of its Social Climate Plan22. At most 37.5% of these costs may go to temporary direct income support for households, so most of the money must go to measures with a lasting effect, such as building renovation, clean heating or zero-emission transport23. The state keeps the remaining ETS2 revenue and must use it for climate purposes, giving priority to social impacts24.
With the Fund, measurement decides. The Commission pays out the money only if the state meets the targets of its plan, and these must include a reduction in the number of households in energy poverty25. Energy poverty, however, cannot be measured directly. Statisticians estimate it with indicators that count as energy poor, for example, a household with a low income and at the same time high energy costs. Each indicator defines “high costs” differently, and that is exactly what matters.
We studied how the indicators respond to support for households with a model that carries the effects of ETS2 on prices and incomes across the whole economy through to the budgets of 3,233 households from household surveys. Together they represent all Czech households. Unlike simple estimates, which merely apply higher prices to today’s consumption, households in the model respond to changes in prices and incomes in the way the data on their spending show. The model also tracks their savings and debts, so it captures how a renovation is financed, and for every result we report how precisely the data can measure it26.
We compared what happens when the same €745 million over 2028 to 2032 goes to insulation and heat pumps and, for comparison, to direct payments to households27. The main finding is that what the indicators record depends as much on how they are constructed as on the policy itself28. Three examples show this.

A direct payment brings households relief. But they spend part of the money on heating, and an indicator that judges high costs by the level of energy spending reads this as a deterioration. As a result, 87% of the relief disappears from it29. It is rather like the scales for someone who has started exercising: they show more kilograms even though the person is in better shape.
Insulation and heat pumps reduce energy poverty, as measured by indicators that combine low income and high costs, by 7.1 to 10.5%. They change the house itself, so their effect lasts: three years after the programme ends, the reduction is still at least 5.4%30.
How it is paid for matters too. An indicator that tracks a household’s savings as well as its income and costs records whether the household paid its share of a renovation from savings or with a loan. If it draws on its savings, the indicator counts this as a deterioration: for a heat pump, the fall in savings wipes out 36% of the improvement brought by lower bills31. The same renovation can therefore come out better or worse simply depending on how it was paid for.

The official indicators, meanwhile, move by only fractions of a percentage point under every programme32. Goals and measurement rules therefore need to be set before the money starts to flow, and instead of a single number we should track several indicators, each with its precision33.

title: ETS2: do we know what we want to measure and achieve?
text:
Where ETS2 money should go
Support that changes the house itself keeps working after the payments stop. ETS2 money should work the same way across the whole economy: it should reduce dependence on imported fuels for good.
The revenue the state keeps from ETS2 may already be used, among other things, for renewable energy, transmission grids and other technologies that contribute to the transition to a safe and sustainable low-carbon economy34. These provisions do not mention nuclear power explicitly. Revenue from the existing allowance system for industry and power generation, ETS1, has gone mainly to the State Environmental Fund since this year. According to the Ministry of the Environment, it is to fund, for example, new renewable sources, the modernisation of heating plants, energy savings and support for low- and middle-income households35.
I would apply the same logic to ETS2, and more boldly. Most of the money from allowances should strengthen the resilience of the economy as a whole, that is, finance our own energy sources, both nuclear and renewable, and the grids that connect them. The Draghi report, too, counts on both kinds of sources with low running costs36. A smaller part should go to targeted support for the households hit hardest by ETS2. According to our model, these are mainly households heating with gas and pensioners living alone37.
China shows that it is possible to invest in one’s own energy sources on a large scale. In 2025 alone, according to the International Energy Agency, it added almost 500 gigawatts of renewable capacity, more than 60% of global growth38. Such investments are, however, expensive. For the two new units at Dukovany the state will pay the Korean company KHNP CZK 407 billion at current prices39, and in August this year the Minister of Industry, Karel Havlíček, acknowledged that, including the cost of money, they will cost CZK 600 to 700 billion40. Construction is to be covered by a state loan, which the European Commission has been examining in depth since December 202541.

title: ETS2: do we know what we want to measure and achieve?
section: The answer to our opening question
text:
The answer to our opening question
So what should we aim for? In my view, greater self-sufficiency in energy, and production that rules do not make unnecessarily expensive. The way there is a mix of three steps: ease the regulations that make products unnecessarily expensive, in Brussels and at home; direct ETS2 revenue mainly into our own energy sources and grids; and help the households hit hardest by ETS2 in a way that lowers their bills for good. Throughout, the state should serve citizens and businesses, not the other way round: if it needs certain data, it should obtain them itself rather than shifting that obligation onto households and firms.
And how will we know we have succeeded? When price swings on world markets feed through to household bills only very slightly. Such a yardstick tracks directly what we care about, and unlike energy poverty indicators it does not depend on whether a household paid for its renovation from savings or with a loan.

      Bridging the Gap: A Novel M2/LIHC Hybrid Indicator Unveils Energy Poverty Dynamics – Case Study of the Czech Republic
      Spoluautoři: Milan Ščasný
      IES Working Papers č. 6/2025
      
        
        
        
        
          Abstrakt
          This paper introduces a novel composite energy poverty indicator, the M2LIHC, which combines elements of the twice-median expenditure share (2M) and Low Income High Cost (LIHC) measures. Using a unique dataset merging the Czech Household Budget Survey and EU-SILC data from 2017-2022, we demonstrate how this hybrid approach provides new insights into energy poverty dynamics. The M2LIHC indicator addresses key limitations of existing metrics, avoiding the LIHC measure’s counterintuitive response to income changes in the lowest decile and mitigating the 2M indicator’s potential overestimation of energy poverty among higher-income households with high energy costs. Our comparative analysis reveals significant differences in energy poverty rates and household characteristics identified by each indicator. The M2LIHC measure proves more robust to income fluctuations than LIHC while maintaining sensitivity to both income and energy cost components. We find energy poverty in the Czech Republic has increased across all indicators from 2017 to 2022, with the M2LIHC indicator suggesting a rise from 8.9% to 13.5%. To further validate our approach, we employ the DASMOD (Distributional And Social Impact Model) to simulate various energy and climate policy scenarios. These simulations demonstrate the complex effects of compensation policies on energy poverty measures, with M2LIHC providing a more nuanced view of policy impacts. By providing a more comprehensive and theoretically consistent measure of energy poverty, coupled with policy simulation capabilities, the M2LIHC indicator offers policymakers an improved tool for targeting support and assessing the effectiveness of energy poverty alleviation strategies in the context of energy transitions and climate policies.

      Publication Bias and Model Uncertainty in Measuring the Effect of Class Size on Achievement
      Spoluautoři: Tomáš Havránek, Zuzana Irsova a Milan Ščasný
      Journal of Labor Economics V tisku
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstrakt
          Class size reduction mandates are routinely justified by studies reporting positive effects on student achievement. Yet other studies report no effects, and the literature as a whole awaits correction for potential publication bias. Moreover, if identification drives results systematically, the relevance of individual studies will vary. We build a sample of 2,819 estimates collected from 66 studies and for each estimate classify 42 factors that reflect estimation context. We employ nonlinear techniques for publication bias correction and model averaging techniques to address model uncertainty. The results are consistent with little publication bias. The implied class size effect is negligible for all identification approaches except Tennessee’s Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio project and for all contexts except classes of fewer than 15 students.

      Elasticity of marginal utility of consumption: the equal-sacrifice approach applied for the Czech Republic
      Spoluautoři: Milan Ščasný
      The Journal of Economic Inequality, 24(1), 261–281
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstrakt
          We provide the first estimate of the elasticity of marginal utility of consumption, μ, for a post-transition economy in the Central & Eastern European region – the Czech Republic – based on household-level data. Using the absolute equal-sacrifice income tax approach, we obtain a central estimate of μ at 1.47, which varies between 1.32 to 1.66 within the study period covering 2005–2022. Moreover, the estimate of the elasticity of marginal utility of consumption differs between various income groups, indicating that this approach is suitable only for those who pay income tax. Including the non-taxpayers segment means ceteris paribus negative μ, and hence its smaller value for the entire population. Importantly, the μ estimate increases when social benefits are included in gross income, and it decreases when social and health insurance contributions are included in the definition of taxes. Since parameter μ is a crucial component of the social discount rate, our result provides useful input for policies that affect intertemporal allocations.

          Abstrakt
          Meta-analysis is how science takes stock of its vast research output. The advent of increasingly capable artificial intelligence (AI) promises an unprecedented ability to identify and synthesize relevant research and its findings. In this document, the meta-analysis of economics research network (MAER-Net) updates existing Reporting Guidelines to be consistent with community-driven best practices for the responsible use and disclosure of AI-assistance in meta-analysis research. This update is meant to further improve the transparency, replicability, and quality of meta-analyses by building upon the 2020 and 2013 Reporting Guidelines published by this Journal. Cook et al.       Volumetric choice experiments and welfare measures in a subsidy-driven context
      Spoluautoři: Wiktor Budziński, Mikołaj Czajkowski a dalších 10
      Resource and Energy Economics, 86, článek 101572
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstrakt
          Volumetric Choice Experiments (VCE) offer a novel approach to studying individual behavior, traditionally explored through Discrete Choice Experiments. This study assesses the efficacy of VCE in understanding farmers' preferences regarding new results-based and practice-based agri-environmental contracts, using a comprehensive international stated preference survey. Recognizing that farmers often act as households maximizing utility rather than purely profit-driven producers, we provide justification for applying a utility-based framework in this context. The subsidy-driven nature of agri-environmental contracts poses a challenge for the use of multiple discrete-continuous choice models suited for VCE data. Conventionally, these models utilize an income-based budget equation, which would not be binding given the willingness-to-accept format of the experiment. To operationalize our model, we adopt a land-based budget equation, facilitating the development of a novel compensating variation measure for welfare analysis. Our findings reveal insightful contrasts between VCE-derived data and traditional DCE results, highlighting the complexities encountered and the comparability of outcomes. By delving into the distinct attributes of VCE and justifying the utility-based approach for farmers, this research not only bridges a critical gap in the literature but also enhances our understanding of farmer behavior, with significant implications for the design and implementation of future agri-environmental policies.

      Conventional wisdom, meta-analysis, and research revision in economics
      Spoluautoři: Sebastian Gechert, Bianka Mey a dalších 7
      Journal of Economic Surveys, 39(3), 980–999
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstrakt
          Over the past several decades, meta-analysis has emerged as a widely accepted tool to understand economics research. Meta-analyses often challenge the established conventional wisdom of their respective fields. We systematically review a wide range of influential meta-analyses in economics and compare them to “conventional wisdom.” After correcting for observable biases, the empirical economic effects are typically much closer to zero and sometimes switch signs. Typically, the relative reduction in effect sizes is 45%–60%.

          Abstrakt
          This study examines the impact of agricultural support on crop diversity measured by a diversity index. Our results indicate that agricultural subsidies have a limited effect on agricultural biodiversity. By using unique farm-level data, we show that subsidies support the income of farmers rather than the agricultural biodiversity. The results are robust regarding the size, practice management and altitude of the agricultural holdings' operations and various measures of agricultural biodiversity.       The impact of the Brexit vote on UK financial markets: a synthetic control method approach
      
      Empirica, 48(2), 559–587
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstrakt
          We estimate how the UK financial markets would have evolved if the Remain camp had won the referendum. To construct the counterfactual, we use the synthetic control method. Our results suggest that there would not have been any significant change in the development of the FTSE 100 Index in the medium to long term if there had not been a referendum. On the other hand, we find a significantly negative effect of 1.2 percentage points on the 10-year bond yield. Given the geopolitical circumstances in mid 2016, financial agents investing in the pound could have sought safer investment options represented by longer-term government bonds, which consequently could result in lower bond yields.

      The Impact of EU Accession on Farm Production in the Czech Republic: A Synthetic Control Method Approach
      
      Czech Journal of Economics and Finance, 70(3), 281–307
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstrakt
          Czech farmers experienced an enormous exogenous shock when they joined the common agricultural market (CAM) and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) in 2004. Using the World Bank's dataset, we apply the synthetic control method to establish a counterfactual case of the Czech Republic food production index in the absence of the CAM and CAP. The results show that the Czech Republic would have had a higher food index if it had not entered the CAM and CAP. Moreover, we show that the CAP and CAM had different impacts on farms in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, which have the most comparable agriculture according to the results of the synthetic control method.

      Quantifying the Effects of the CNB's Exchange Rate Commitment: A Synthetic Control Method Approach
      
      Czech Journal of Economics and Finance, 67(6), 539–577
      
        
        
        Video
        
        
        
          Abstrakt
          In this paper I evaluate the quantitative effects of the Czech National Bank's commitment to keep the Koruna from appreciating that were put in place in 2013. I focus on the policy's impact on output, unemployment, and inflation. I use the synthetic control method, which allows me to compute the counter-factual development of the Czech economy in the absence of the commitment. I find that the commitment helped decrease unemployment substantially. The effect on overall output is also strongly positive, almost 2 percentage points for growth in 2015, but only marginally statistically significant, which might be connected to disturbances created by changes in excise taxes. The effect of the commitment on inflation is positive but not statistically significant at standard levels.

title: ETS2: víme, co chceme měřit a čeho dosáhnout?
text:
Od roku 2028 začne Evropská unie zpoplatňovat emise CO₂ z vytápění budov a z pohonných hmot. Povolenky v novém systému ETS2 nebudou kupovat domácnosti, ale dodavatelé paliv1. Náklady se však promítnou do cen: podle našeho výpočtu zaplatí průměrná česká domácnost v roce 2032 kvůli ETS2 za energie o 218 eur ročně víc, necelé procento svého čistého příjmu2. EU start systému letos o rok odložila3 a Česko s Itálií teď prosazují jeho pozastavení4.
Pokud ETS2 začne platit, získá stát z prodeje povolenek nové příjmy, které musí použít na klimatická a sociální opatření5. Než rozhodneme, co s nimi, měli bychom mít jasno ve dvou věcech: čeho chceme dosáhnout a podle čeho poznáme, že se to povedlo. Na první otázku odpovídá situace, v jaké se Evropa nachází. U druhé pomůže náš výzkum: ukazatele, podle kterých se bude úspěch posuzovat, mohou stejnou pomoc vyhodnotit velmi různě.

title: ETS2: víme, co chceme měřit a čeho dosáhnout?
text:
Čeho chceme dosáhnout
Snižovat emise CO₂ je rozumný cíl. Evropa ho ale sleduje z horší výchozí pozice než její konkurenti.
Energie je v Evropě drahá a většinu jí dovážíme. Draghiho zpráva o budoucnosti evropské konkurenceschopnosti z roku 2024 uvádí, že firmy v EU platí za elektřinu dvakrát až třikrát víc než v USA a za zemní plyn čtyřikrát až pětkrát víc. Za hlavní příčinu označuje nedostatek vlastních přírodních zdrojů, ale také vady společného trhu s energií a vysoké daně. A varuje, že pokud Evropa své politiky nesladí, hrozí, že dekarbonizace půjde proti konkurenceschopnosti a růstu6. V roce 2024 EU dovezla 57 % energie, kterou měla k dispozici, a dvě třetiny dovozu tvořila ropa a ropné produkty7.
Hlavní konkurenti si stejné náklady neukládají. Spojené státy od ledna 2026 nejsou součástí Pařížské dohody8 a vyhlásily „národní energetickou nouzi“, aby rozšířily domácí výrobu energie včetně ropy a zemního plynu9. Čína má trh s povolenkami, firmám ale zatím neurčuje, kolik smějí vypustit celkem10.
K drahé energii se přidává regulace. Podle Draghiho zprávy ji více než 60 % firem v EU považuje za překážku investic11. V letech 2019 až 2024 přijala EU zhruba 13 tisíc aktů, zatímco v USA vzniklo na federální úrovni asi 3 500 zákonů a 2 000 rezolucí12. Souhrnné číslo o tom, o kolik regulace evropské výrobky zdražuje, chybí13. Dílčí odhady ale existují: chemický průmysl stála legislativa EU z let 2004 až 2014 zhruba 2 % tržeb a 12 % přidané hodnoty, tedy zhruba každé osmé euro, které odvětví samo vytvořilo14.
Část regulace si přidáváme sami. Předsedkyně Evropské komise Ursula von der Leyenová letos v říjnu navrhla „pakt proti nadměrné regulaci“: členské státy by měly ukázat, které povinnosti pocházejí z práva EU a které si přidaly samy15. Česko se u nových zákonů zlepšilo: podle vládní metodiky z roku 2016 přebírá směrnice v minimální podobě a neodůvodněné přitvrzování z nových zákonů téměř zmizelo16. Zůstává ale ve starších předpisech, v poslaneckých pozměňovacích návrzích a v praxi17. Například při prodeji nebo pronájmu budovy postavené a naposledy větší měrou upravené před rokem 1947 se průkaz energetické náročnosti nemusí pořizovat, pokud se na tom obě strany písemně dohodnou18. Podle analýzy AMO ale média a firmy zpracovávající posudky takové výjimky často zamlčují19. Výjimky, které lidem ušetří administrativu, jsou správné; lidé se o nich však musí dozvědět. Administrativa přitom podle Hospodářské komory stojí české podnikatele zhruba 72 miliard korun ročně20.
Čeho tedy chceme dosáhnout? Aby EU i Česko méně závisely na dovozu fosilních paliv, což je správné i bez ohledu na klima, a aby výrobky vyrobené v Evropě zbytečně nezdražovaly předpisy. Peníze z ETS2 k tomu mohou přispět, záleží ale na tom, kam půjdou a podle čeho se bude posuzovat jejich přínos.

title: ETS2: víme, co chceme měřit a čeho dosáhnout?
section: Jak poznáme, že se to daří
text:
Jak poznáme, že se to daří
Pravidla pro peníze z ETS2 mají dvě části. Část výnosů jde do evropského Sociálního klimatického fondu, ze kterého může Česko v letech 2026 až 2032 získat až 50 miliard korun21. Stát k tomu musí přidat nejméně čtvrtinu nákladů svého Sociálního klimatického plánu22. Na dočasnou přímou podporu příjmů domácností smí jít nejvýše 37,5 % těchto nákladů, většina tedy musí jít do opatření s trvalým účinkem, jako jsou renovace budov, čisté vytápění nebo bezemisní doprava23. Zbývající výnosy z ETS2 si stát ponechá a musí je použít na klimatické účely, přednostně s ohledem na sociální dopady24.
U fondu přitom rozhoduje měření. Komise peníze vyplácí, jen pokud stát plní cíle svého plánu, a mezi nimi musí být i snížení počtu domácností v energetické chudobě25. Energetickou chudobu ale nelze změřit přímo. Statistici ji odhadují pomocí ukazatelů, které za energeticky chudou považují například domácnost s nízkým příjmem a zároveň vysokými náklady na energie. Co přesně jsou „vysoké náklady“, určuje každý ukazatel jinak, a právě na tom záleží.
Jak ukazatele na pomoc domácnostem reagují, jsme zkoumali v modelu, který promítá dopady ETS2 na ceny a příjmy v celé ekonomice do rozpočtů 3 233 domácností z výběrových šetření. Ty dohromady zastupují všechny české domácnosti. Na rozdíl od jednoduchých odhadů, které vyšší ceny jen přepočítají na dnešní spotřebu, domácnosti v modelu na změny cen a příjmů reagují tak, jak to ukazují data o jejich výdajích. Model sleduje i jejich úspory a dluhy, takže zachytí, jak se renovace financuje, a u každého výsledku uvádíme, jak přesně ho data dokážou změřit26.
Porovnali jsme, co se stane, když stejných 745 milionů eur v letech 2028 až 2032 půjde na zateplení a tepelná čerpadla, a pro srovnání i na přímé platby domácnostem27. Hlavní zjištění zní: to, co ukazatele zaznamenají, závisí na jejich konstrukci stejně jako na samotné politice28. Ukazují to tři příklady.

Přímá platba domácnostem uleví. Část peněz ale utratí za teplo, a ukazatel, který vysoké náklady posuzuje podle výše výdajů za energie, si to vyloží jako zhoršení. Z úlevy v něm tak zmizí 87 %29. Dopadne to podobně jako s váhou u člověka, který začal cvičit: ukáže víc kilogramů, přestože je na tom lépe.
Zateplení a tepelná čerpadla snižují energetickou chudobu měřenou ukazateli, které kombinují nízký příjem a vysoké náklady, o 7,1 až 10,5 %. Mění samotný dům, a proto jejich účinek trvá: ještě tři roky po skončení programu je pokles nejméně 5,4 %30.
Způsob placení hraje roli také. Ukazatel, který vedle příjmu a nákladů sleduje i úspory domácnosti, zaznamená, zda domácnost zaplatila spoluúčast na renovaci z úspor, nebo z půjčky. Když sáhne do úspor, vyhodnotí to jako zhoršení: u tepelného čerpadla tak úbytek úspor smaže 36 % zlepšení, které přinesly nižší účty31. Stejná renovace tak může vyjít lépe nebo hůř jen podle toho, jak byla zaplacena.

Oficiální ukazatele se přitom u všech programů pohnou jen o zlomky procentního bodu32. Cíle a pravidla měření je proto potřeba stanovit dřív, než peníze začnou proudit, a místo jednoho čísla sledovat několik ukazatelů, každý i s jeho přesností33.

title: ETS2: víme, co chceme měřit a čeho dosáhnout?
text:
Kam s penězi z ETS2
Pomoc, která mění samotný dům, působí i po skončení plateb. Podobně by měly působit i peníze z ETS2 v celé ekonomice: trvale snižovat závislost na dovážených palivech.
Výnosy, které si stát z ETS2 ponechá, smí už dnes jít mimo jiné na obnovitelné zdroje, přenosové sítě a další technologie přispívající k přechodu na bezpečnou a udržitelnou nízkouhlíkovou ekonomiku34. Jaderné zdroje tato ustanovení výslovně nezmiňují. Výnosy ze stávajícího systému povolenek pro průmysl a energetiku, ETS1, jdou od letošního roku převážně do Státního fondu životního prostředí. Podle ministerstva z nich půjdou peníze například na nové obnovitelné zdroje, modernizaci tepláren, úspory energie i podporu domácností s nižšími a středními příjmy35.
Stejnou logiku bych uplatnil i u ETS2, a to odvážněji. Většina peněz z povolenek by měla posilovat odolnost ekonomiky jako celku, tedy financovat vlastní zdroje energie, jaderné i obnovitelné, a sítě, které je propojí. S oběma druhy zdrojů s nízkými provozními náklady počítá i Draghiho zpráva36. Menší část by měla jít na cílenou pomoc domácnostem, které ETS2 zasáhne nejvíc. Podle našeho modelu jsou to hlavně domácnosti, které topí plynem, a osaměle žijící důchodci37.
Že se do vlastních zdrojů dá investovat ve velkém, ukazuje Čína. Jen v roce 2025 v ní podle Mezinárodní energetické agentury přibylo téměř 500 gigawattů obnovitelných zdrojů, přes 60 % celosvětového přírůstku38. Takové investice jsou ale drahé. Za dva nové bloky v Dukovanech zaplatí stát korejské firmě KHNP 407 miliard korun v současných cenách39 a ministr průmyslu Karel Havlíček letos v srpnu připustil, že i s cenou peněz vyjdou na 600 až 700 miliard korun40. Stavbu má pokrýt státní půjčka, kterou od prosince 2025 podrobně prověřuje Evropská komise41.

title: ETS2: víme, co chceme měřit a čeho dosáhnout?
text:
Odpověď na úvodní otázku
Čeho bychom tedy měli chtít dosáhnout? Podle mě větší soběstačnosti v energetických zdrojích a výroby, kterou zbytečně nezdražují předpisy. Vede k tomu mix tří kroků: uvolnit regulace, které výrobky zbytečně zdražují, v Bruselu i doma; posílat výnosy z ETS2 hlavně do vlastních zdrojů energie a sítí; a domácnostem, které ETS2 zasáhne nejvíc, pomáhat tak, aby jim natrvalo klesly účty. Stát by přitom měl sloužit občanům a firmám, nikoli naopak: pokud potřebuje určité údaje, měl by si je opatřit sám, a nepřenášet tuto povinnost na domácnosti a podniky.
A jak poznáme, že se to povedlo? Podle toho, že se výkyvy cen na světových burzách promítnou do účtů domácností jen velmi málo. Takové měřítko sleduje přímo to, o co nám jde, a na rozdíl od ukazatelů energetické chudoby nezávisí na tom, zda domácnost zaplatila renovaci z úspor, nebo z půjčky.

      Bridging the Gap: A Novel M2/LIHC Hybrid Indicator Unveils Energy Poverty Dynamics – Case Study of the Czech Republic
      with Milan Ščasný
      IES Working Papers No. 6/2025
      
        
        
        
        
          Abstract
          This paper introduces a novel composite energy poverty indicator, the M2LIHC, which combines elements of the twice-median expenditure share (2M) and Low Income High Cost (LIHC) measures. Using a unique dataset merging the Czech Household Budget Survey and EU-SILC data from 2017-2022, we demonstrate how this hybrid approach provides new insights into energy poverty dynamics. The M2LIHC indicator addresses key limitations of existing metrics, avoiding the LIHC measure’s counterintuitive response to income changes in the lowest decile and mitigating the 2M indicator’s potential overestimation of energy poverty among higher-income households with high energy costs. Our comparative analysis reveals significant differences in energy poverty rates and household characteristics identified by each indicator. The M2LIHC measure proves more robust to income fluctuations than LIHC while maintaining sensitivity to both income and energy cost components. We find energy poverty in the Czech Republic has increased across all indicators from 2017 to 2022, with the M2LIHC indicator suggesting a rise from 8.9% to 13.5%. To further validate our approach, we employ the DASMOD (Distributional And Social Impact Model) to simulate various energy and climate policy scenarios. These simulations demonstrate the complex effects of compensation policies on energy poverty measures, with M2LIHC providing a more nuanced view of policy impacts. By providing a more comprehensive and theoretically consistent measure of energy poverty, coupled with policy simulation capabilities, the M2LIHC indicator offers policymakers an improved tool for targeting support and assessing the effectiveness of energy poverty alleviation strategies in the context of energy transitions and climate policies.

      Publication Bias and Model Uncertainty in Measuring the Effect of Class Size on Achievement
      with Tomáš Havránek, Zuzana Irsova and Milan Ščasný
      Journal of Labor Economics Forthcoming
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstract
          Class size reduction mandates are routinely justified by studies reporting positive effects on student achievement. Yet other studies report no effects, and the literature as a whole awaits correction for potential publication bias. Moreover, if identification drives results systematically, the relevance of individual studies will vary. We build a sample of 2,819 estimates collected from 66 studies and for each estimate classify 42 factors that reflect estimation context. We employ nonlinear techniques for publication bias correction and model averaging techniques to address model uncertainty. The results are consistent with little publication bias. The implied class size effect is negligible for all identification approaches except Tennessee’s Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio project and for all contexts except classes of fewer than 15 students.

      Elasticity of marginal utility of consumption: the equal-sacrifice approach applied for the Czech Republic
      with Milan Ščasný
      The Journal of Economic Inequality, 24(1), 261–281
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstract
          We provide the first estimate of the elasticity of marginal utility of consumption, μ, for a post-transition economy in the Central & Eastern European region – the Czech Republic – based on household-level data. Using the absolute equal-sacrifice income tax approach, we obtain a central estimate of μ at 1.47, which varies between 1.32 to 1.66 within the study period covering 2005–2022. Moreover, the estimate of the elasticity of marginal utility of consumption differs between various income groups, indicating that this approach is suitable only for those who pay income tax. Including the non-taxpayers segment means ceteris paribus negative μ, and hence its smaller value for the entire population. Importantly, the μ estimate increases when social benefits are included in gross income, and it decreases when social and health insurance contributions are included in the definition of taxes. Since parameter μ is a crucial component of the social discount rate, our result provides useful input for policies that affect intertemporal allocations.

          Abstract
          We estimate the elasticity of marginal utility of consumption (μ) for Europe and 32 individual European countries using household-level income tax data. Specifically, we rely on the absolute equal-sacrifice approach to elicit the revealed preferences of income taxpayers on their political preference for income redistribution. Our central estimate of μ equals 1.43. With few exceptions, μ’s for European countries exceed unity, ranging between 1.2 and 1.94. We discuss the implications of our estimates for inequality measurement, benefit transfer, and the social discount rate.

      Reporting Guidelines for Meta-Analysis in Economics—Updated for AI
      with Nikolai Cook, František Bartoš and 10 others
      Journal of Economic Surveys
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstract
          Meta-analysis is how science takes stock of its vast research output. The advent of increasingly capable artificial intelligence (AI) promises an unprecedented ability to identify and synthesize relevant research and its findings. In this document, the meta-analysis of economics research network (MAER-Net) updates existing Reporting Guidelines to be consistent with community-driven best practices for the responsible use and disclosure of AI-assistance in meta-analysis research. This update is meant to further improve the transparency, replicability, and quality of meta-analyses by building upon the 2020 and 2013 Reporting Guidelines published by this Journal. Cook et al. (2026) describe the guiding principles behind the update. Future meta-analyses, whether or not they use AI, are expected to follow these updated guidelines or to be prepared to give reasons if they deviate from them.

      Volumetric choice experiments and welfare measures in a subsidy-driven context
      with Wiktor Budziński, Mikołaj Czajkowski and 10 others
      Resource and Energy Economics, 86, Article 101572
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstract
          Volumetric Choice Experiments (VCE) offer a novel approach to studying individual behavior, traditionally explored through Discrete Choice Experiments. This study assesses the efficacy of VCE in understanding farmers' preferences regarding new results-based and practice-based agri-environmental contracts, using a comprehensive international stated preference survey. Recognizing that farmers often act as households maximizing utility rather than purely profit-driven producers, we provide justification for applying a utility-based framework in this context. The subsidy-driven nature of agri-environmental contracts poses a challenge for the use of multiple discrete-continuous choice models suited for VCE data. Conventionally, these models utilize an income-based budget equation, which would not be binding given the willingness-to-accept format of the experiment. To operationalize our model, we adopt a land-based budget equation, facilitating the development of a novel compensating variation measure for welfare analysis. Our findings reveal insightful contrasts between VCE-derived data and traditional DCE results, highlighting the complexities encountered and the comparability of outcomes. By delving into the distinct attributes of VCE and justifying the utility-based approach for farmers, this research not only bridges a critical gap in the literature but also enhances our understanding of farmer behavior, with significant implications for the design and implementation of future agri-environmental policies.

      Conventional wisdom, meta-analysis, and research revision in economics
      with Sebastian Gechert, Bianka Mey and 7 others
      Journal of Economic Surveys, 39(3), 980–999
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstract
          Over the past several decades, meta-analysis has emerged as a widely accepted tool to understand economics research. Meta-analyses often challenge the established conventional wisdom of their respective fields. We systematically review a wide range of influential meta-analyses in economics and compare them to “conventional wisdom.” After correcting for observable biases, the empirical economic effects are typically much closer to zero and sometimes switch signs. Typically, the relative reduction in effect sizes is 45%–60%.

Our results indicate that agricultural subsidies have a limited effect on agricultural biodiversity. By using unique farm-level data, we show that subsidies support the income of farmers rather than the agricultural biodiversity. The results are robust regarding the size, practice management and altitude of the agricultural holdings' operations and various measures of agricultural biodiversity.       The impact of the Brexit vote on UK financial markets: a synthetic control method approach
      
      Empirica, 48(2), 559–587
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstract
          We estimate how the UK financial markets would have evolved if the Remain camp had won the referendum. To construct the counterfactual, we use the synthetic control method. Our results suggest that there would not have been any significant change in the development of the FTSE 100 Index in the medium to long term if there had not been a referendum. On the other hand, we find a significantly negative effect of 1.2 percentage points on the 10-year bond yield. Given the geopolitical circumstances in mid 2016, financial agents investing in the pound could have sought safer investment options represented by longer-term government bonds, which consequently could result in lower bond yields.

      The Impact of EU Accession on Farm Production in the Czech Republic: A Synthetic Control Method Approach
      
      Czech Journal of Economics and Finance, 70(3), 281–307
      
        DOI
        
        
        
          Abstract
          Czech farmers experienced an enormous exogenous shock when they joined the common agricultural market (CAM) and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) in 2004. Using the World Bank's dataset, we apply the synthetic control method to establish a counterfactual case of the Czech Republic food production index in the absence of the CAM and CAP. The results show that the Czech Republic would have had a higher food index if it had not entered the CAM and CAP. Moreover, we show that the CAP and CAM had different impacts on farms in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, which have the most comparable agriculture according to the results of the synthetic control method.

      Quantifying the Effects of the CNB's Exchange Rate Commitment: A Synthetic Control Method Approach
      
      Czech Journal of Economics and Finance, 67(6), 539–577

          Abstract
          In this paper I evaluate the quantitative effects of the Czech National Bank's commitment to keep the Koruna from appreciating that were put in place in 2013. I focus on the policy's impact on output, unemployment, and inflation. I use the synthetic control method, which allows me to compute the counter-factual development of the Czech economy in the absence of the commitment. I find that the commitment helped decrease unemployment substantially. The effect on overall output is also strongly positive, almost 2 percentage points for growth in 2015, but only marginally statistically significant, which might be connected to disturbances created by changes in excise taxes. The effect of the commitment on inflation is positive but not statistically significant at standard levels.
